1.note: The psalmist is using the term **soul** to mean his entire person from the perspective of his spiritual and emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [myself] or [my inner being]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were **clothed with splendor and majesty**. He means that Yahweh possesses splendor and majesty just as a king might wear magnificent robes. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternatively, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you are splendid and majestic]

The terms **splendor** and **majesty** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [extreme magnificence]

The expression **you are clothed with splendor and majesty** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [you are splendid and majestic]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **splendor** and **majesty**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [you are splendid and majestic]

2.note: The psalmist is making a comparison to describe how God wears light. The point of this comparison is that just as **a garment** covers and adorns a person, so **light** covers and adorns God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [putting light around you as though it were a garment]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a tent curtain** is stretched out to provide shelter, so the **heavens** are stretched out by God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [spreading out the heavens as a man would spread out a tent curtain]

3.note: The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were **setting his upper chambers on the waters**. This image pictures God’s dwelling place as being built above the sky, where the rain clouds are. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [It is as though you have set the upper chambers of your home on the waters in the sky]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a king or mighty warrior who rode across the sky with **the clouds** serving as his **chariot**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [It is as though you ride the clouds like chariots]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were someone who could **walk on the wings of the wind**. He means that Yahweh moves about freely and swiftly, as if he were riding on the wind itself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you move about freely as though you were flying along with the wind]

4.q: עֹשֶׂ֣ה מַלְאָכָ֣י⁠ו רוּח֑וֹת מְ֝שָׁרְתָ֗י⁠ו אֵ֣שׁ לֹהֵֽט
4.note: In these clauses, the subjects and objects are not marked, and could fill either role. They could mean: (1) Yahweh makes the winds his messengers and he makes flaming fire his servants, as in the ULT, or (2) Yahweh makes his messengers winds and he makes his servants flaming fire. Alternate translation: [making his messengers winds, and his servants, flaming fire]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were **making the winds his messengers**. This image means that Yahweh uses the winds to carry out his purposes, just as a king would send messengers to accomplish his will. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [sending the winds as he would send his messengers]

The psalmist is speaking of **flaming fire** as if it were a person who could serve God. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [controlling flaming fire so that it serves him]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [making flaming fire his servants]

5.note: The psalmist is speaking of **the earth** as if Yahweh had placed it **upon** physical **foundations** like a building is constructed on a foundation. The psalmist means that Yahweh created the world to be stable and secure. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He made the earth to be stable]

If your language does not use this passive form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [never can anyone move it]

6.note: The psalmist assumes that readers will know that **the deep** refers to the waters of the ocean or the primeval waters that once covered the earth. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [with deep water]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a garment** completely covers a person, so **the deep** completely covered the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as completely as if that were its clothing]

The psalmist is speaking of **the waters** as if they were a living thing that could stand in a certain position. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the waters were higher than the mountains]

7.note: These two phrases **From your rebuke they fled** and **from your voice of thunder they hurried away** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could combine the phrases. Alternate translation: [From your thunderous rebuke they fled away]

The psalmist is speaking of **the waters** as if they were living things that could **flee** and **hurry away**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they receded … they went away]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe a **voice** that is characterized by **thunder**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your thunderous voice]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh’s **voice** as if it were **thunder** to express how loud it is. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your loud voice]

8.note: **They** refers to “the waters” from verse 6. This reflects the idea from Genesis 7:11 that the flood waters came from where they had been stored both above the firmament and underground. Here it is saying that after the flood God returned the waters to those places, so some of it **ascended the mountains** to return to the heavens and some **descended the valleys** to return to their places underground.

Some translations take **the mountains** to be the subject of **ascended** and **the valleys** to be the subject of **descended**. This makes it difficult to translate the following verse however, since verse 9 continues to refer to the waters as “they.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to follow what it does here. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to follow the ULT. Alternate translation: [The mountains rose; the valleys descended]

9.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the waters. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the waters]

10.note: **The one** in verses 10, 13, and 14 refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, you send]

11.note: The pronoun **They** refers to the springs (mentioned in the previous verse). It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The streams of water give drink to]

The psalmist is using **break their thirst** as a common expression to mean “quench their thirst” or “satisfy their thirst by drinking.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [quench their thirst] or [drink and are satisfied]

12.note: The pronoun **them** refers to the streams of water mentioned in verse 10. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Alongside the streams of water]

The psalmist is using **they give voice** as a common expression of his culture to mean “they sing” or “they chirp.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they chirp]

13.note: The psalmist is using the phrase **The one watering** to refer to God without using a pronoun. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a name or pronoun to clarify the referent. Alternate translation: [Yahweh waters]

The psalmist is speaking of the sky as if it were **upper chambers** in a building from which God sends rain down on the mountains. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from high in the sky]

Here, **fruit** could be both literal and figurative. It could mean either of these things or both: (1) The work of watering the mountains produces literal fruit, which satisfies the creatures on earth. The next two verses list some of that fruit. Alternate translation: [this work of yours produces fruit, which satisfies the earth] or (2) The result of watering the mountains is that the earth is satisfied with the water. Alternate translation: [because you do this, the earth is satisfied]

Here, **the earth** represents the creatures that live on the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the earthly creatures are satisfied]

14.note: The phrase **The one** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, who makes grass grow]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from earlier in the verse if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and the one making plants grow]

Here, **to bring forth** marks **bread from the earth** as the goal or purpose of **plants for the work of man**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [in order to produce]

The psalmist is using one kind of food, **bread**, to represent food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [food]

15.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And by providing wine]

Here the **heart** represents a person’s inner self, including their emotions and sense of well-being. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all mankind] or [everyone]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **face**. He means faces in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [to make people’s faces shine]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [he gives olives to make the face shine]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and by providing bread]

16.note: The psalmist is speaking of **the trees of Yahweh** as if they were living things that could be satisfied. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The trees of Yahweh get plenty of rain]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from earlier in the verse if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the cedars of Lebanon which he planted are satisfied]

17.note: The expression **where birds make their nests there** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in many languages. The word **there** repeats the idea of **where**. If this would be unnatural in your language, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [where birds make their nests]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **stork**. He means storks in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [storks, cypress trees their home]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the stork makes the cypress tree her home]

18.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the high mountains are the home for the wild goats]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from earlier in the verse if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the cliffs are a refuge for the hyraxes]

A **hyrax** is a kind of small, furry animal that lives in rocky areas. If your readers would not be familiar with what a hyrax is, you could use the name of a similar animal that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [for the rock badgers]

19.note: The pronoun **He** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh made]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that the **appointed times** are the festivals and religious observances that are determined by the phases of the moon. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to indicate the times for the special days of each month]

The psalmist is speaking of **the sun** as if it were a living thing that could know when to set. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you made the sun to set at the proper time each night]

20.note: The psalmist uses **and** to indicate that **it is night** is the result of God setting **darkness**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [and night happens] or [which creates night]
The pronoun **it** refers to the darkness. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [in the night]

21.note: The psalmist is speaking of the young lions as if they were **seeking their food from God**. He means that God provides food for the lions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as though they are asking God to give them their food]

22.note: The psalmist assumes that readers will know that he means that the young lions retreat because **the sun rises** and it becomes daytime. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [When the sun rises]

23.note: The terms **work** and **labor** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [to all of his work that he does]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **Man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Each person]

24.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wisdom**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [wisely] or [skillfully]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **creation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what you have created]

25.note: The terms **great** and **broad of hands** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [enormous in size]

The psalmist is using **broad of hands** as a common expression of his culture to mean that the shores of the sea are far apart. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and with distant shorelines]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that **great** refers to the sea’s vast size or extent. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [large]

The psalmist says **there is no number** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [and there are too many to count]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the small living things are there with the great living things]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that **great** refers to the large size of some of the sea creatures. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [large]

The psalmist is using the adjectives **small** and **great** as nouns to mean small creatures and large creatures. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you could translate these words with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [small ones with large ones]

The psalmist is referring to all of the living creatures in the sea by naming two extremes, **small** and **great**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [of every size together]

26.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Leviathan travels there]

27.note: The pronoun **them** refers to all of the living creatures that the psalmist has been describing, including the sea creatures mentioned in the previous verses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [All of these living creatures]

The psalmist is speaking of creatures depending on God for their food as if they were physically looking at someone for help. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [need you]

28.note: The psalmist assumes that readers will know that it is when God provides the food that the creatures gather it. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [When you give to them; then they gather it]

The psalmist is using **you open your hand** as a common expression of his culture to mean “you give generously.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you give generously]

The adjective **good** is functioning as a noun, referring to good things (specifically, good food that God provides). If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this with a noun phrase or indicate what kind of good things are meant. Alternate translation: [they are satisfied with the good food]

29.note: The psalmist assumes that readers will know that it is when God hides his face from his creatures that they then become terrified. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [When you hide your face; then they are terrified]

The psalmist is using **You hide your face** as a common expression of his culture to mean “You withdraw your care” or “You turn away from them.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [When you ignore them]

The expression **they are terrified** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [that terrifies them]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that it is when God takes the breath away that creatures then expire. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [When you take away their breath; then they expire]

The psalmist is using **return to their dust** as a common expression of his culture to mean “die and decay.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and turn into dirt]

30.note: The psalmist assumes that readers will know that it is when God sends out his breath that creatures then begin to live. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [When you send out your breath; then they are created]

The same word that is translated as **breath** in this and the previous verse also means “spirit.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to translate as it does. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to translate as the ULT does. Alternate translation: [You send out your Spirit; they are created]

The expression **they are created** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [you create them]

Here, **the face of the land** represents everything living on the surface of the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [everything living on the earth]

31.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [May his creatures honor Yahweh forever]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **creation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in what he has created]

32.note: The phrase **the one** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh looks at the earth]

The psalmist uses **and** to indicate that **it shakes** is the result of God **looking at the earth**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [the one looking at the earth, so that it shakes]

The psalmist uses **and** to indicate that **they smoke** is the result of God touching **the mountains**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [he touches the mountains, which causes them to smoke]

33.note: The psalmist is using this possessive form to describe his relationship with God. The phrase **my God** indicates the God whom the psalmist worships and serves. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to the God whom I worship]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the idea of **existence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [while I am alive]

34.note: By **my meditation**, the psalmist is probably referring to the things that he has expressed in this psalm. If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **meditation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the things that I have expressed]

The psalmist is speaking of his **meditation** as if it were something that could have a sweet taste. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May my meditation please him]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I will rejoice** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize his personal commitment to rejoice in Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [For my part, I will rejoice]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a location that the psalmist could be **in**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because of who Yahweh is]

35.note: The psalmist is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean wicked people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you could translate this word with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and wicked people]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from earlier in the verse if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and may the wicked be no more]

The psalmist is using the term **soul** to mean his entire person from the perspective of his spiritual and emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [myself] or [my inner being]

The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]
